title: The Great EV Recalibration
gist: Andrew Miller argues that post-IRA Western battery investment has failed to loosen China's grip (cells 79%→83%, anode 92%, cathode 88%) while Western automakers retreat with $50bn+ in EV write-downs. Rather than an 'own everything' strategy, he urges selective allied scaling, licensing/joint production (Tesla-Panasonic, Ford-CATL) and next-gen chemistry bets like GM's LMR cells, framing the contest as one of setting terms for cooperation with China.

insights.claim: Despite capital flowing into Western supply chains after the Inflation Reduction Act, China's share of global lithium-ion cell production rose from 79% in the year the act passed to 83% last year.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: IRA-driven reshoring has not dented China's cell share — skepticism warranted on Western cell-capacity build-out narratives.
insights.locator: The capital that poured into western supply chains

insights.claim: Battery demand outside China more than doubled from 331 GWh to 958 GWh over the same period that China's global cell share rose.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Ex-China demand growth is being met largely by Chinese supply, sustaining import dependence.

insights.claim: China made 92% of the world's battery anode material and 88% of its cathode material last year, and every Western retreat widens that gap.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Upstream midstream concentration remains extreme — any trade restriction on anode/cathode would bite hardest.

insights.claim: Benchmark's October battery price assessment put a high-nickel NCM811 cell at about $75/kWh in China versus $82 in North America and $89 in Europe; the author says whether Chinese costs are artificially low is academic for a carmaker choosing a supplier this quarter.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: A ~9-19% cell cost gap keeps procurement flowing to Chinese suppliers regardless of subsidy debates.
insights.quote: Whether Chinese costs are artificially low is a fair question. For a carmaker choosing a supplier this quarter, it is academic.

insights.claim: China's EV output grew elevenfold in five years, from 1.4 million in 2020 to 15.1 million last year, and Chinese producers launched more than 115 new models this year versus 64 from non-Chinese producers.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Chinese OEM product cadence nearly doubles non-Chinese rivals — pressure on legacy automaker share and margins.
insights.locator: The speed and scale of China's EV ramp-up

insights.claim: Where markets are open to Chinese cars EVs sell: four in five EVs sold last year in Latin America, the Middle East, Oceania and Africa were built in China.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Emerging markets without tariff barriers are effectively Chinese EV territory.
insights.locator: And where markets open the door

insights.claim: China's shift from upstream battery supplier to direct automotive competitor means Western carmakers can no longer simply buy from the cheapest and most abundant producer, which is the core of the 'great EV recalibration'.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Sourcing decisions are now geopolitical — expect continued tariffs and localisation requirements shaping supplier choice.
insights.locator: This is the heart of the great EV recalibration

insights.claim: The 2027 Chevrolet Bolt, starting under $30,000 and the cheapest new EV in America, reaches that price using LFP cells from CATL, illustrating that the West can build the car but China builds what makes it affordable.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Affordable Western EVs remain dependent on Chinese LFP cells — CATL is embedded in the US low-cost segment.
insights.quote: the West can build the car, but China still builds what makes it affordable.

insights.claim: Europe has failed to build a battery base sufficient for its car industry: Northvolt went bankrupt, Freyr abandoned Norway, and the working plants on the continent rely on CATL and LGES.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: European homegrown cell makers have failed; Asian incumbents capture the European cell market.

insights.claim: One in five EVs sold in Europe last year was built in China and more than two in five ran on cells from Chinese makers, as Asian-run plants kept EVs cheaper at the cost of regional control.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Europe's legacy automakers face Chinese competition at both vehicle and cell level, driving further protectionist legislation.
insights.locator: Those facilities have kept EVs cheaper

insights.claim: Stellantis, Ford, GM and Volkswagen wrote down more than $50bn on EV plans and three of them walked away from battery joint ventures; Stellantis sold its stake in a Canadian battery venture to LG Energy Solution for $100.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Western OEM retreat transfers battery assets cheaply to Asian incumbents like LGES, consolidating their position.
insights.quote: Stellantis sold its stake in a Canadian battery venture to LG Energy Solution for $100
insights.locator: Yet the West is stepping back

insights.claim: Western carmakers cannot price their way into the EV market without owning more of the battery value chain behind it, even though the 2021-24 tailwinds for supply chain spending have gone.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: OEMs that abandon vertical integration risk structural cost disadvantage versus Chinese rivals.
insights.quote: Western carmakers have learned the hard way that you cannot price your way into this market without owning more of the chain behind it.
insights.locator: Western carmakers have learned the hard way

themes.theme: Selective strategy: tech bets and licensing

insights.claim: GM took a $6bn charge but kept investing in cells; its lithium manganese-rich (LMR) cells due in 2028 promise about a third more energy density than LFP at similar cost, which the author calls the right kind of bet.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Watch GM's 2028 LMR launch as a test of whether Western chemistry innovation can sidestep Chinese LFP dominance.
insights.quote: That is the right kind of bet: technology built for the supply chain in front of you, instead of a race to catch up with established technologies.

insights.claim: An 'own everything' battery strategy takes too long and costs too much for Western governments; they should instead back the parts of the chain where domestic or allied suppliers can credibly scale and provide carmakers a real second source.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Policy support likely concentrates on select chain segments — favours allied suppliers in credible niches over broad full-chain plays.

insights.claim: Where technical, financial or time barriers are too great, licensing or joint production with incumbents may be the only route to onshoring battery manufacturing and skills, as Tesla did with Panasonic in Nevada and Ford is doing with CATL in Michigan.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Licensing deals with Chinese cell makers (CATL-style) may expand despite political friction — beneficial for licensors' royalty streams.
insights.quote: working with that supply base may be the fastest way to displace it in the future

insights.claim: Chasing every link of the battery chain would spread Western capital so thin that incumbents already in control would stay in control; the West is unlikely to make every battery it needs.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Diffuse capital allocation across the chain is a losing strategy — favour concentrated bets.
insights.locator: The West can move some steps

insights.claim: The West holds leverage because China wants access to large car markets it has yet to crack while the West needs China's supply chain; whichever side sets the terms of cooperation first will decide the next stage of the EV race.
insights.speaker: Andrew Miller
insights.so_what: Watch market-access-for-investment deals (e.g. Chinese cell plants in exchange for EV access) as the key policy lever.
insights.quote: The question is not whether to compete or cooperate, but on what terms.
